title: AI early warning system to detect deadly infection
full_text:
A new artificial intelligence “traffic light” system to help identify and evaluate the risk of a deadly infection quicker will be rolled out in emergency departments across Western Sydney.
The AI tool named “SAFE-WAIT” is a prediction model that helps clinicians evaluate the risk of sepsis sooner, by taking a patient’s vital signs, which then use an algorithm to identify which are most at risk and should be urgently treated in an ED.
The system works like a traffic light system, as the program indicates whether the patient is at low, moderate or high risk of sepsis, assisting staff to determine how urgent care is required.
Sepsis is a life-threatening medical emergency that happens when your body has an extreme, toxic response to an infection, and can rapidly become serious.
According to Sepsis Australia, more than 84,000 people per year are impacted by sepsis across the country, with 12,000 deaths annually due to the infection.
The expansion comes after a successful pilot at Westmead Hospital demonstrated the algorithm detected high-risk sepsis cases 90 minutes faster than traditional triage techniques, and helping avoid patients entering severe septic shock.
The state government is backing the project through a share of $4.9m in funding. It will be rolled out at five hospital EDs including Westmead, Auburn, Blacktown, Mount Druitt, and Nepean hospitals over the next two and a half years.
Health Minister Ryan Park said the government was excited to see it expand to the other hospitals, following the great trial results.
Associate Professor Dr Amith Shetty, who led the charge on the model said to train, build and validate the algorithm prior to the trial, they used anonymised data from approximately a million patient records, which were collected between 2017 and 2019 from the electronic medical record systems in Western Sydney hospitals. Dr Shetty said that with the overflowing ED’s in the region, and how hidden the infection can be – the system dramatically helps health officials.
